title: Many people ignore these ‘early red flags’ in romance scams, says Harvard-trained psychologist
description: Most people want a romantic relationship that makes them feel seen, understood and accepted. Romance scammers exploit that desire, trying to manufactu
body: Most people want a romantic relationship that makes them feel seen, understood and accepted. Romance scammers exploit that desire, trying to manufacture a bond quickly so they can gain access to money or sensitive information.As a clinical psychologist who has worked with couples and individuals for over a decade, I've seen some of the smartest people be deceived by well-honed tactics designed to lower their defenses. Genuine intimacy is built slowly through consistent action, shared experiences and a willingness to be flawed and vulnerable. Scammers, on the other hand, rely on urgency, the performance of vulnerability and emotional shortcuts to get what they want. Here are five signs you might be dealing with a scammer, and how to spot the difference between a real connection and calculated manipulation.1. Their emotions don't match the weight of what they're sharingA common sign of emotional manipulation is a mismatch between the content of what someone says and their emotional delivery. To create a false sense of instant intimacy, scammers might prematurely disclose something deeply traumatic. Pay close attention to how they share it.When someone genuinely opens up about something painful or challenging in their life, it usually coincides with some natural hesitation, vulnerability or awkwardness. With a scammer, the emotion might feel like an artificial layer they pasted onto a rehearsed script. They might appear way too comfortable, polished or even at ease when delivering such personal stories to someone they barely know.You may be watching a performance designed to make you drop your guard and reciprocate. Because the disclosure is so heavy, many people feel guilty when doubt creeps in, so they will silence their concerns. But if something strikes you as inauthentic, listen to your gut.2. They escalate the relationship at warp speedA real connection requires time for a person to earn your trust and a place in your life. Manipulators, on the other hand, often push for exclusivity with urgency. They are quick to use labels like "soulmates" and employ tactics like future-faking — for example, talking about trips, moving in or having children together — within days or weeks.This isn't someone who is swept up in passion. It's a strategic tactic used to bypass your critical thinking skills. They flood you with an emotional buffet of everything you've been starving for, through constant attention, intense communication, flattery and early grand declarations. Through these actions, they induce an intense emotional high that makes you overlook inconsistencies, red flags or warning signs. If someone claims you're the love of their life before they even know what you're like on a bad day, they're much more likely to be operating from their own agenda.3. Their life is an endless string of convenient crisesEvery relationship has its share of unexpected stressors, but with a manipulator, drama and emergencies are a core feature of their ploy. Specifically, the crises are always happening just out of your sight, so you can't necessarily verify them. For example, their lack of consistency might be explained away by a last-minute canceled flight, a problem with their bank or a family emergency that requires immediate help.Don't get sucked into these crises. Instead, focus on the pattern of the process. Each crisis conveniently prevents you from either meeting other people in their life, verifying their story or seeing them in normal, unscripted settings. More importantly, they condition you to step into a rescuer role. They are trying to normalize your willingness to devote money and time to keep them afloat as some test of your loyalty and commitment to the relationship.4. You have no access to their real relationships and routinesHealthy partners who want to create a genuine and lasting connection will want to bring you into their world. Over time, they'll introduce you to their family, friends, co-workers, gym routine, etc. Their ecosystem will feel full, and they'll take concrete steps to integrate you into it. When someone is running a scam, their entire life feels just out of reach, almost like it's operating in a vacuum. They might keep you far away from the people who actually know them, offer vague or changing details about their work and background, or insist that you keep your relationship private. Somehow they'll weaponize this privacy as a way of protecting the relationship and keeping what you have special. Secrecy is often the glue that keeps manipulation schemes together. If you can't see how they exist and operate in the world outside of their relationship with you, you're only seeing a curated aspect of them.5. Your intuition can sense something is off, even when everything looks great on paperWhen someone sweeps you off your feet, is attentive and tells you everything you want to hear, it's easy to talk yourself out of what you know in your gut. Many people ignore early red flags because they don't want to seem cynical, paranoid or ungrateful. They want to believe in the love and connection that's being fostered.Authentic relationships make you feel safe, calm and increasingly clear-headed over time. Manipulators will often leave you feeling anxious, confused and rushed. If you find yourself constantly rationalizing their behavior or explaining contradictions in their stories, pay attention.Ultimately, the best way to protect yourself from being scammed is to refuse to skip the foundational steps that real trust is built on. In new relationships, slow down the pace, verify their lofty words with consistent action, and pay attention to whether their vulnerability feels lived-in or rehearsed. Genuine connection never requires you to abandon your basic gut instincts to prove your devotion.Sabrina Romanoff is a Harvard-trained clinical psychologist, professor, and writer specializing in relationships, high-achievement, and anxiety, with a private practice in New York City. She has been featured in The New York Times, Forbes, Women's Health, USA Today, and on CBS and ABC. Follow her on Instagram @DrSabrinaRomanoff.

schema.headline: Many people ignore these ‘early red flags’ in romance scams, says Harvard-trained psychologist

title: FAA issues nationwide ground stop citing communication issues affecting ‘multiple’ air traffic control facilities
description: An American Airlines passenger plane taxis at Los Angeles International Airport (LAX) in Los Angeles, California, on Oct. 23, 2026. Caroline Brehman |
body: An American Airlines passenger plane taxis at Los Angeles International Airport (LAX) in Los Angeles, California, on Oct. 23, 2026. Caroline Brehman | AFP | Getty ImagesThe Federal Aviation Administration issued a nationwide ground stop on Friday afternoon, disrupting hundreds of flights, after reporting communication problems affecting "multiple" air traffic control centers.The issues were related to communications and radar issues, according to an internal message from Alaska Airlines, which was seen by CNBC.A ground stop halts flights at their departure point."The FAA issued a nationwide ground stop for all U.S. airports following communication issues impacting multiple Air Route Traffic Control Centers," the FAA said.The agency said in a statement that "FAA technicians are investigating the issue."Inbound international flights will be managed on a case by case basis, the FAA said. Nationwide ground stops are extremely rare. In January 2023, the FAA halted flights because of issues with a pilot alert system. Before that, traffic was halted nationwide after the Sept. 11, 2001, terror attacks.This is breaking news. Please refresh for updates.

schema.headline: FAA issues nationwide ground stop citing communication issues affecting ‘multiple’ air traffic control facilities

title: AI risks are the biggest threat to the financial system, Fed survey finds
description: Signage on a fence at the Nscale data center project in Barstow, Texas, on Oct. 15, 2026.Eli Hartman | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesThreats from artificial
body: Signage on a fence at the Nscale data center project in Barstow, Texas, on Oct. 15, 2026.Eli Hartman | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesThreats from artificial intelligence topped the list for greatest risks to the financial system, far exceeding any other dangers, according to respondents who participated in a Federal Reserve survey released Friday.The central bank's twice-yearly look at a variety of dangers saw a surge in respondents saying that the biggest danger comes from AI along several fronts including debt, stock market valuations and security risks."Respondents noted three distinct areas of concern: (1) elevated equity valuations and the possibility that lower-than-expected earnings could result in lower valuations and a market correction; (2) cybersecurity risk, stemming from either a malicious attack by sophisticated state actors or damage caused by frontier AI models themselves; and (3) risks associated with complex forms of AI-related financing," the report stated.The report comes with Wall Street on edge over high-flying AI hyperscalers, while communities are on alert for the rapid spread of data centers used to power the technology. Some 56% of voters in this month's midterm elections said data centers were of crucial or major importance in their choices, according to exit polling.Respondents to the Fed survey released Friday include a variety of market participants, economists, analysts and institutional sources. The report covers the period up to Oct. 28, just a few days shy of the election.Of the group, 87% cited AI as a "salient risk" to the system. That was up from 50% in the survey during the spring of this year and well ahead of the next most-cited danger, a risk asset correction, which was mentioned by 52% of those surveyed. Other leading risks were higher long-term rates (48%), cyberattacks (43%) and fiscal debt sustainability (43%), the latter coming with the U.S. debt over $40 trillion and the budget deficit near $2 trillion.The report otherwise found the system fairly stable, though it mentioned that hedge fund leverage is at its highest since 2013 and concentrated on a relatively small group.

schema.headline: AI risks are the biggest threat to the financial system, Fed survey finds

title: They train people to avoid 'honeypot' scams—here are the common red flags they spot: 'It feels so good to be wanted'
description: Shawnee Delaney often kicks off a training session by telling a room full of corporate workers: "OK, raise your hand if you've ever gotten a flatterin
body: Shawnee Delaney often kicks off a training session by telling a room full of corporate workers: "OK, raise your hand if you've ever gotten a flattering message on LinkedIn just complimenting your background and your profile and your experience.""Every hand goes up," she says. Then, she tells attendees how responding to a simple adulatory message could unwittingly open the door to a potential romance scam.Delaney is a corporate security expert, well-versed in teaching people how to avoid “honeypot” schemes, in which a bad actor uses romantic or sexual interest to build trust and gain information, access or leverage over a target. The term is currently making headlines in the wake of former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's resignation from the company, following reporting on his admitted affair with an alleged Chinese spy.Honeypots, also known as "honey traps," are a very human form of social engineering attack, a category that also includes various forms of phishing and use of deepfake technology. And you don't have to be a billionaire tech CEO to possess information that scammers may value.As competition in the global artificial intelligence race heats up, OpenAI is reportedly training employees to recognize espionage tactics including bribery, romantic manipulation and blackmail, according to The Wall Street Journal. On Nov. 3, cryptocurrency exchange Binance revealed that a recent cyberattack — which saw roughly $6 billion of digital assets stolen — was partially made possible by a fake job interview scheme that infected an employee’s work computer with malware."People can get solicited, bribed, romanced, etc.," says Kevin Tian, co-founder and CEO of Doppel, an AI-powered platform meant to help identify and deflect social engineering attacks. He adds: "If you've got access to sensitive IP [intellectual property] — it's not just AI companies — you can be a target."Increasingly, scammers can use AI to scour websites ranging from Reddit to Pinterest for an individual's personal information and customize a ploy designed specifically for them, Tian says. Once they have relevant data points, attackers tend to use "the oldest tricks in the book: elicitation, flattery, ego," says Delaney, a former intelligence officer with the Defense Intelligence Agency and the founder and CEO of Washington, D.C.-based corporate security consulting firm Vaillance Group.In many cases, Delaney notes, targets have an inkling that something is suspicious — but they'd rather allow themselves to believe the interest is legitimate. So how do you keep yourself from falling victim? Trust your self-awareness, common sense and ability to identify situations that feel too good to be true, she says."The bottom line is, we're all human," says Delaney, adding: "It feels so good to be wanted, or to be respected, or to be appreciated, or loved."How to spot red flags and do some vettingDelaney, who has worked with Fortune 500 companies such as Uber and Merck, advises corporate clients on cybersecurity risks and develops training programs to improve employees' awareness of security threats. Her sessions aim to build awareness of manipulative connections, such as romance scams, from how they begin to the natural progression they often take. "Introduction, then repeated contact, favors, sensitive requests — the secrecy, the pressure," she says.Bad actors may tap into any information you post online to find an interest that can be mirrored and exploited, or an acquaintance who can be infiltrated and make an introduction. If someone you know and trust makes an introduction, you might be less likely to "go do due diligence" on the new person, even if they're a stranger, Delaney says.One of Vaillance's services includes building a "targeting package" around an executive or C-Suite member, says Delaney. "We can show how they are vulnerable and how we would target that organization just by leveraging the people around them in that circle: spouses, friends, kids, parents, administrative assistants, neighbors," she says. "That's when people's eyes open."From there, she discusses red flags to spot. Conversations that begin with flattery and seemingly innocuous small talk can gradually shift toward digging for information, introductions to colleagues or access to documents, says Delaney. It's human nature to want to be helpful and fulfill friendly requests, she adds. Add a potential romantic connection to the mix, especially amid an ongoing "loneliness epidemic," and the urge to comply can be even harder to resist, she says.Shawnee Delaney's Vaillance Group creates security plans and offers training programs for large organizations.Source: Shawnee DelaneyIf you feel yourself getting cornered in a situation where a recent acquaintance or romantic partner keeps asking for information you're not comfortable revealing, Delaney says it helps to have first practiced polite refusal. "One of my favorites is: They could just respond with: 'Why do you ask?'" she says. "Put the other person on the defensive. You could give a nondescript answer. You can say you don't know. You can say you can't respond."If you're ever suspicious of a new connection — even if you don't want to be — do yourself a favor and conduct some basic vetting, she recommends. You might examine their social media profiles and other publicly available information, for example, to see if their story checks out.If you can't find enough information to allay your suspicions, don't be shy about alerting your employer's security or human resources team, she says. For smaller companies, or scams outside the workplace, you can file a complaint for cyber threats or romance scams with the Federal Bureau of Investigation's Internet Crime Complaint Center.And pay attention if your new paramour starts asking you specific questions about your finances or work credentials, says Delaney."If you have no game at home, and you get off an airplane somewhere and suddenly everyone's all over you, we call that a red flag," she says.

schema.headline: They train people to avoid 'honeypot' scams—here are the common red flags they spot: 'It feels so good to be wanted'

title: ‘We will sue them’: Canada threatens Stellantis as Trump trade war reshapes Jeep production plans
description: Industry Minister Melanie Joly addresses media at Sheraton Center Toronto Hotel following sale of Stellantis, November 12, 2026.Sophie Bouquillon | To
body: Industry Minister Melanie Joly addresses media at Sheraton Center Toronto Hotel following sale of Stellantis, November 12, 2026.Sophie Bouquillon | Toronto Star | Getty ImagesCanada has threatened to sue auto giant Stellantis over the planned sale of an idled assembly plant in Brampton, Ontario, alleging breaches of a federal funding agreement after the carmaker announced plans to shift production to the U.S. amid President Donald Trump's trade war.Speaking at a news conference on Thursday, Industry Minister Mélanie Joly said the government had served Stellantis with a formal notice of default, giving the company 30 days to address its concerns or face legal action."We sent a notice of default and, basically, they have 30 days — or else, of course, we will sue them," Joly told reporters in Toronto. Joly said Stellantis had violated its contractual commitments to the Canadian government and the workers at Brampton by announcing an agreement to sell the plant to armored vehicle manufacturer Roshel earlier in the week. She added that the company was now "on the hook" for hundreds of millions of dollars over the move.Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has described the situation at the Brampton plant as "unacceptable" and a "betrayal" of its workers.The standoff comes as the U.S. and Canada remain locked in a bitter trade dispute, with Trump repeatedly putting pressure on automakers to move vehicle production south of the border. Stellantis, which owns auto brands including Dodge, Fiat, Chrysler and Peugeot, had scrapped plans to build its Jeep Compass at the Brampton plant and shifted future production to a factory in Illinois amid U.S. auto tariffs and other market pressures. Stellantis Canada CEO Trevor Longley said in a statement shared with CNBC that the company would return $24 million it received in government support for the Brampton Assembly's original retooling plan. This amount, however, falls significantly short of the Canadian government's own estimate of what the company owes.  Stock Chart IconStock chart iconNew York-listed shares of Stellantis year-to-date. "We recognize the disappointment and uncertainty surrounding the future of the facility. While our decision to sell the plant represents a change from the original plans for Brampton, the agreement we have advanced with a Canadian manufacturer provides a path to return the facility to productive industrial use," Longley said.   "As Canada's largest automotive employer, this decision also allows Stellantis to focus its resources on sustaining competitive manufacturing operations in Canada in the face of challenging market realities," he added. Jeep Grand Cherokee SUVs at a dealership in Mississauga, Ontario, Canada, on Friday, Oct. 17, 2025.Bloomberg | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesStellantis said Monday that it had agreed to sell the Brampton assembly plant to Roshel for an undisclosed amount. It also acknowledged its obligations to employees at the facility and said it remains prepared to work with Unifor, Canada's largest private sector union, to negotiate a settlement to assist union-represented employees. Stellantis stock has fallen sharply since the start of the year, with its Milan-listed shares down more than 60% for 2026 so far. — CNBC's Michael Wayland contributed to this report.

schema.headline: ‘We will sue them’: Canada threatens Stellantis as Trump trade war reshapes Jeep production plans

title: Trump says he wants to ‘get Cuba done’ before leaving office, would consider military force
description: US President Donald Trump speaks during a press briefing in the Brady Briefing Room of the White House in Washington, DC, on Nov. 9, 2026. Mandel Ngan
body: US President Donald Trump speaks during a press briefing in the Brady Briefing Room of the White House in Washington, DC, on Nov. 9, 2026. Mandel Ngan | AFP | Getty ImagesU.S. President Donald Trump has said he wants to "get Cuba done" before leaving office in 2029, adding that he would "certainly consider" military intervention against the communist-run Caribbean island.In an interview with conservative radio host Hugh Hewitt on Thursday, Trump said his administration was monitoring the situation in Havana "very closely" and described Cuba as a "failed" state."I want to get Cuba done before I leave," Trump said. His comments marked the first time he has put a timeline on possible military intervention to topple Cuban authorities, according to Politico. Trump said Secretary of State Marco Rubio, whose parents are from Cuba, "would love to do it" and said he would "certainly consider" a short military operation.It comes as the U.S. continues to enforce a comprehensive economic embargo against Cuba, a campaign which has contributed to a deepening energy and economic crisis on the island. Cuba has suffered repeated nationwide blackouts in recent months, as well as fuel and food shortages.  The Cuban Embassy in Washington, D.C., estimated on Thursday that the cost of the U.S. blockade to Cuba between March 2025 and February 2026 amounted to $8 billion.Earlier this month, the Treasury Department imposed further sanctions on Cuban oil tankers and shipping companies and threatened to target any international entity or person doing business within its marine or maritime industries as part of a push "to end the Cuban regime's malign activities, both in Cuba and across our hemisphere." A tank truck drives on a street in Matanzas, Cuba on March 30, 2026.Stringer | Afp | Getty ImagesIn response, Cuba's Embassy in Washington, D.C., said these steps "deepen an energy siege that already leaves hospitals without reliable power and families facing blackouts. The blockade is not targeted at a government. It is collective punishment that hits ordinary people every day."Trump has previously talked up the prospect of a "friendly takeover" of Havana and said the White House could turn its sights on Cuba after the Iran war. The U.S. president has also said he could do anything he wanted with the country, adding that he thinks he will have the "honor" of "taking Cuba." In May, Cuban Energy Minister Vicente de la O Levy said the country of roughly 10 million had run out of fuel oil and diesel, describing the country's predicament as "extremely tense." Analysts have typically been skeptical about the prospect of a U.S. military campaign against Cuba, suggesting that further economic pressure against the island's authorities appears more likely.

schema.headline: Trump says he wants to ‘get Cuba done’ before leaving office, would consider military force

title: Wholesale prices rose 0.3% in October, putting annual rate at 6.5%, the highest in nearly four years
description: Wholesale prices increased less than expected in October, but inflation pressures persisted and the Federal Reserve is likely still on target for an i
body: Wholesale prices increased less than expected in October, but inflation pressures persisted and the Federal Reserve is likely still on target for an interest rate increase soon.The producer price index, which measures the prices domestic producers get for their products before they reach the consumer, rose a seasonally adjusted 0.3% for the month, against the Dow Jones consensus for a 0.4% increase, the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported Friday.Stripping out food and energy, core PPI posted a 0.3% gain, meeting expectations.On an annual basis, headline PPI accelerated 6.5%, up 0.2 percentage point for the highest annual rate since November 2022.The report comes just a few weeks ahead of the Federal Reserve's next policy meeting, Dec. 8-9. Markets are fully pricing in a quarter percentage point increase in the central bank's key overnight borrowing rate, with slight odds that the Federal Open Market Committee might opt for a half-point hike.Stock market futures added to gains following the release while Treasury yields were mixed.Earlier this week, the BLS reported that inflation at the cash register was hotter than expected.The headline consumer price index saw a 0.4% increase in October while core was up 0.3%, both 0.1 percentage point higher than expected. Because of the government shutdown in October 2025, the BLS couldn't collect some data and refrained from putting out a 12-month inflation figure for CPI. However, the figures showed that the Fed remains a good distance from its 2% inflation goal."Today's PPI data – which shows some signs of improving, albeit still too-high – is unlikely to change the Fed's approach in December because the CPI data was already outside their comfort zone," said Chris Zaccarelli, chief investment officer for Northlight Asset Management.Moreover, policymakers are beginning to worry that inflation generated by the Iran war and higher fuel prices, along with President Donald Trump's tariffs, are beginning to spread through the economy. The Fed generally would look through such price pressures as temporary, but the breadth of inflation could indicate that inflation is becoming more entrenched."We've had some signs of trouble now for several months in a row," Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee said in a CNBC interview Friday. "If you look at how broad-based the inflation is, it's not just that we're above the target and have been for some time. It's that in categories that are not driven by oil prices and not driven by tariffs, you're still seeing stalled progress and in some cases going the wrong way."Stripping out food, energy and trade services, PPI saw an increase of 0.5% in October.Goods prices increased 0.5% in October, with more than 60% of that move driven by goods excluding food and energy, which actually saw a 0.1% decrease. On an annual basis, the goods index jumped 10.2%, the biggest 12-month surge since October 2022.Final demand services prices increased 0.2%, most of which was linked to transportation and warehousing services, and within that category a 3.9% gain in truck transportation of freight. "We've been above 2% for almost six years, and while it sometimes we were making progress, lately we're not making any progress, and if anything, it's going the wrong way," Goolsbee said. "Inflation is rising; it's proved far more persistent than we predicted at the beginning from the supply shocks."Other items in the PPI report also showed multiyear gains. Prices for intermediate processed goods soared 14.6% from October 2025, the biggest annual gain since July 2022. Intermediate prices for services posted a 6.9% increase, the most since November 2022.

schema.headline: Wholesale prices rose 0.3% in October, putting annual rate at 6.5%, the highest in nearly four years

title: Hassett denies report he's leaving White House: 'Not true'
description: watch nowNational Economic Council Director Kevin Hassett on Friday poured cold water on a report that he's expected to leave the White House in the c
body: watch nowNational Economic Council Director Kevin Hassett on Friday poured cold water on a report that he's expected to leave the White House in the coming weeks.That report is "not true," Hassett told CNBC's Eamon Javers in a text message.Semafor reported earlier Friday afternoon that Hassett "has been inquiring about roles outside the administration," even before Republicans' drubbing in last week's midterm election.Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, and his counselor David Zervos, are among the names being floated to replace Hassett, according to Semafor, which cited unnamed people familiar with his plans.But a White House official told CNBC in a statement later Friday, "There is no factual basis for this reporting.""Kevin Hassett is a key member of President Trump's economic team and will continue working to advance President Trump's economic policies," the official said on condition of anonymity to discuss the matter.Zervos, reached by phone after Semafor's story published, declined to comment.While Hassett denies he is departing the White House, several other Trump administration officials have stepped down since Democrats' staggering wins in the Nov. 3 midterm, flipping Congress blue and overhauling President Donald Trump's plans for the rest of his term.White House chief of staff Susie Wiles left her role Friday and was succeeded by Stephen Miller. Multiple Department of Justice officials have also left since Election Day, including Harmeet Dhillon, a leader in the DOJ's civil rights division, and John Eisenberg, who headed the national security division.

schema.headline: Hassett denies report he's leaving White House: 'Not true'

title: 10-year Treasury yield moves to 5.17% as traders weigh producer price report
description: Traders work on the floor at the New York Stock Exchange (NYSE) in New York, US, on Monday, March 9, 2026. Michael Nagle | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesThe
body: Traders work on the floor at the New York Stock Exchange (NYSE) in New York, US, on Monday, March 9, 2026. Michael Nagle | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesThe 10-year Treasury yield stayed over 5% on Friday after October's producer price index, a measure of wholesale prices, came in slightly less than expected. The yield — the key benchmark for mortgages, auto loans and credit card debt — rose 4 basis points to 5.143%. It reached a high of 5.174% earlier in the day.The 2-year Treasury note yield, typically more sensitive to short-term Federal Reserve interest rate decisions, was lower by less than 1 basis point at 4.859%. The longer-dated 30-year Treasury bond yield, sensitive to geopolitical risks, was more than 4 basis points higher at 5.472%. One basis point equals 0.01%, and yields and prices move in opposite directions.October's producer price index rose 0.3% versus September, less than the 0.4% expected by economists polled by Dow Jones. But on an annual basis, PPI rose 6.5% over the past 12 months, the biggest annual increase since November 2022.There was "no silver lining" in the inflation report, said Chris Rupkey, chief economist at FWDBONDS, adding that core PPI — which excludes  food, energy and trade services — increased 0.5% in October."It is economics 101 that producer prices lead consumer prices and right now it looks like consumers will be on the hook for a fresh burst of factory inflation," he said.The moves come after 10-year Treasury yields jumped more than 13 basis points to more than 5% in Thursday's session, with the 2-year yield soaring more than 15 basis points.Investors now see a Federal Reserve rate hike next month as a certainty. Traders are pricing in 100% odds of a rise at the Dec. 9 meeting, according to the CME Group's FedWatch tool. Odds of a quarter percentage point hike now stand at 89%, with the chance of a half point increase at around 14%.Energy inflation remains a key part of the puzzle, with oil posting its second weekly decline as prospects of renewed strikes by the U.S. against Iran fade. U.S. West Texas Intermediate futures for December delivery were down 0.2% at $88.56 per barrel. Brent crude, the international oil benchmark, was higher by 0.02% at $95.84.

schema.headline: 10-year Treasury yield moves to 5.17% as traders weigh producer price report

title: Women are taking pay cuts and 'white-knuckling it' to manage menopause and work: 'I feel like I'm sitting on the sidelines'
description: Around 2020, Amy Terry noticed she didn't feel like her usual self.The 50-year-old Michigander was working as a director of programming at a health as
body: Around 2020, Amy Terry noticed she didn't feel like her usual self.The 50-year-old Michigander was working as a director of programming at a health association when she says she began experiencing symptoms like memory loss, low energy, mental processing difficulties — or, as she describes it, "waking up every day feeling like you were slogging through mud.""I went from being this highly competent professional person to barely being able to get through phone calls," Terry says.As the healthcare system strained under the weight of the Covid-19 pandemic, Terry, like many other people, struggled to get care. When she finally did, she found out it wasn't Covid-19. It was perimenopause.Terry got through a few more years juggling her symptoms with her job, but by 2023, she couldn't hold out any longer. She quit to start independent consulting.Women, and some trans and non-binary people, often experience career setbacks stemming from menopause that can hurt them financially and professionally. Four in 10 women who have experienced menopause or perimenopause say it has negatively affected their life or work, according to a recent survey of over 3,800 U.S. women from Gallup and Melinda French Gates' Pivotal, a group of organizations focused on social progress for women and young people.Of them, roughly 28% felt limited in the effort they could give at work, 15% decided against pursuing a promotion or leadership role, 12% reduced their hours, and 10% took an extended leave from work or didn't return."This isn't just a health issue," says Jasmine Escalera, career expert at resume builder site LiveCareer. "It's a workplace issue."A 2023 Mayo Clinic study estimated menopause symptoms drove $1.8 billion in lost work time per year in the U.S. alone.Perimenopause, the transitional period before menopause, typically begins in one's 40s and can last several years, often bringing symptoms like hot flashes, sleep issues, irritability and lower energy, according to the Office on Women's Health. Menopause typically occurs in one's 50s and marks 12 months since a person's last period, but is often used colloquially to include the preceding perimenopause as well.The timing of menopause can create a perfect storm. It frequently comes at a time in many women's careers when they're breaking into leadership or approaching their peak earning years, which is often between the ages of 35 and 44 for women, according to data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics. It also typically happens when many are caregiving for aging parents or raising children. This can make for an impossible choice for many women."Women have fought so hard for their place in the workforce," says Mimi Wied, who began perimenopause around a decade ago. "They don't want to lose it by looking like they can't handle it."The career consequences for women "may increase the gaps we're trying to decrease," Escalera says, referring to disparities such as those in women's pay and senior-level representation relative to men. "That is a definite talent breakdown."For Terry, becoming an independent consultant cost her employer-sponsored healthcare at the time she most needed it. It also drastically changed her income: She says she took around an 85% pay cut in the transition."These are supposed to be my highest-earning years," Terry says, "and I feel like I'm sitting on the sidelines."'I just have to white-knuckle it'Many women are unprepared for menopause because of social stigma around discussing it, poor health education and dismissal of women's health issues."I've been in the healthcare environment for 30 years; if I can't figure this out, I don't know how anyone can," says Terry.Wied also says she didn't know what to expect. The answer quickly became apparent: The 48-year-old from Brenham, Texas, says she experienced everything from night sweats and sleeplessness to anxiety and rage."Sometimes I didn't feel in control of my own mouth and my body and my actions," she says.Wied left her job as a museum docent for a secretarial role paying roughly $20,000 less when she worried her irritability would affect her capacity to help visitors, she says: "If I could have quit working, I would have."When women do scale back at work because of menopause, they may struggle to regain that professional ground later. Terry's job switch wasn't just downshifting to a part-time role: "It's an entire change in the trajectory of your career," she says.Factors like ageism in the job search for those of menopausal age, as well as the high cost of healthcare, particularly for common menopause treatments like hormone replacement therapy, may keep some women silently struggling through their symptoms at work.Erin Levin is currently working through perimenopause. As a high school English teacher, the 41-year-old from San Jose, California, needs to stay on her A-game because "there is no down moment in teaching," she says.But since starting perimenopause around two years ago, she's experienced brain fog, difficulty sleeping, and heightened anxiety and stress that make her work difficult sometimes, she says. She sometimes struggles with tasks that "were not an issue" for her a few years ago."Now I'm just like, God, why does it just feel so exhausting all the time?" Levin says.Her parents help with childcare some evenings, and she tries not to schedule big tasks first thing in the morning, but it's been an adjustment. Scaling back at work isn't an option financially, she says, as a single mother sharing custody of her child."I still have to maintain the same appearance of having all the same skills and energy level as other people who aren't in my medical position," Levin says. "I just have to white-knuckle it."'I don't want my daughter to have to face any of that'Some women see hope in coming legislation and employer benefits offerings.Last year, Rhode Island became the first state to enact workplace protections for women experiencing menopause. In September, Sens. Kirsten Gillibrand, D-N.Y., and Rick Scott, R-Fla., held the first congressional hearing devoted to menopause. Illinois and the city of Philadelphia have also adopted legislation taking effect in 2027 providing accommodations and protections for those in menopause.In September, a nongovernmental organization, the International Organization for Standardization, published the first standard for developing workplace policies and practices supporting people through menstruation and menopause.Many organizations have a ways to go in providing menopause-related benefits for their employees.In a 2026 study from the Society for Women's Health Research and workplace menopause research organization The Fuchsia Tent, fielded among 1,100 people, around one-third of decision-makers said menopause support is currently in place or actively planned in their workplace. Fewer than 10% of employees said their organization offers menopause-specific support. Respondents said some broader benefits, like flexible scheduling, remote options, and confidential telehealth or virtual care, would also be helpful for menopause.Terry, Wied and Levin said they had to meet with multiple doctors before finding one who'd take their concerns seriously and who'd prescribe them hormone replacement therapy.Levin and Wied each have a daughter. They hope better support and women's healthcare are available for their daughters when they begin menopause."I'm hoping that by the time my daughter goes through this, we'll have a lot more information, a lot more resources, because as it stands, it makes you super angry," Wied says."It's a cost on my energy, it's a cost on my stress levels, it's a cost on my bank account," Levin adds. "I don't want my daughter to have to face any of that."As for Terry, she says she was part of a study examining potential mental health impacts of hormonal fluctuations in perimenopausal women; she hopes the research can help future generations of women. Meanwhile, her switch to independent consulting has offered her greater flexibility and a more manageable workload. But it's not perfect."I'm worried about retirement, I'm worried about having enough money, I'm worried about being able to continue healthcare," she says. "But I also feel like I have to take the time to feel like I'm on solid ground again."

schema.headline: Women are taking pay cuts and 'white-knuckling it' to manage menopause and work: 'I feel like I'm sitting on the sidelines'

title: Jensen Huang scandal casts doubt on Nvidia’s AI dominance — how we got here
description: watch nowNvidia is facing one the biggest crises in its 33 year history, with founder Jensen Huang resigning as CEO Thursday after multiple reported a
body: watch nowNvidia is facing one the biggest crises in its 33 year history, with founder Jensen Huang resigning as CEO Thursday after multiple reported affairs, including one with a woman alleged to be a Chinese spy. Now CFO Colette Kress has taken the helm as Nvidia's interim CEO.The implications of Huang's affair with Alice Huang run far deeper than infidelity. That's because her ties to Nvidia customer Megaspeed put her in the middle of a sprawling effort to accumulate AI chips across Southeast Asia. And Megaspeed is under investigation for possibly diverting restricted Nvidia chips into the hands of Chinese companies.The relationship between Jensen Huang and Alice Huang dates back to 2023, according to The New York Times. That was a "turbulent" period for Nvidia, Jensen Huang told CNBC during an interview at the time. Nvidia was in the midst of redesigning some chips to comply with the first in a series of strict export controls imposed by the U.S. government that restricted sales to China."The regulation is going to be just fine. We're going to be able to work through it," Huang told CNBC from Nvidia's headquarters in February 2023. The interview was for a documentary about how Huang created Nvidia and built it into the backbone of the AI boom.That same day, CNBC also interviewed Kimberly Powell, Nvidia's vice president of healthcare, with whom Jensen Huang reportedly had an affair.It's not the first time Nvidia has faced an uncertain future. The company nearly went bankrupt in the early years after it was founded in 1993."Every company makes mistakes and I make a lot of them," Huang said in the 2023 interview. "And some of them put the company in peril." In the early months of the AI boom, after OpenAI launched ChatGPT in November 2022, Nvidia was on the precipice of historic growth. Jensen Huang told CNBC he'd like to keep running the company for "three or four decades," as long as "I feel that I'm making a real contribution to the company."Less than four years later, Jensen Huang is out, and we're taking a look back at our interviews with the Nvidia co-founder and other company executives as the chipmaker enters this next critical chapter. Watch the video for the full story.WATCH: The rise, reinvention and uncertain future of Nvidia without Jensen Huang

schema.headline: Jensen Huang scandal casts doubt on Nvidia’s AI dominance — how we got here

title: U.S. seizes $1.2 billion in cryptocurrency stolen from Binance
description: Visual China Group | Getty ImagesU.S. authorities have seized around $1.2 billion in virtual assets stolen from cryptocurrency exchange Binance last m
body: Visual China Group | Getty ImagesU.S. authorities have seized around $1.2 billion in virtual assets stolen from cryptocurrency exchange Binance last month, the Department of Justice said Thursday, as it vowed action to tackle cyberscams originating from North Korea. Over $6 billion was stolen from industry giant Binance on Oct. 29, which the DOJ attributed to actors linked to the North Korean military.Collective efforts between the U.S. government and private sector have resulted in more than $2.7 billion of that amount being frozen. The FBI blames the attack, which shook confidence in crypto market security, on members of the North Korean military it refers to as "TraderTraitor." The DOJ said it was taking coordinated action against what it called the North Korean government's "schemes to fund its regime through the massive theft of cryptocurrency."That includes "the court-authorized seizure and restraint of more than $1.2 billion worth of cryptocurrency recently stolen from Binance," it said.watch nowDOJ units, law enforcement partners and virtual asset service providers have been working to intercept the stolen assets.But efforts to track and freeze the assets are ongoing, as TraderTraitor actors continue to launder them through various cryptocurrency channels.Authorities have also seized cloud-based infrastructure used in a massive identity impersonation scam known as "FaceStealer," which has seen more than $400 million worth of cryptocurrency stolen over 18 months, the DOJ said.The scheme sees hackers set up fake video meetings using stolen accounts and recordings of people known to the target by using AI-generated deepfakes. The hackers then say a technical problem requires a fix, install malware on a computer and take over the victim's communications, steal their cryptocurrency and target their contacts — sometimes months or more than a year after the initial compromise.Individuals working in the cryptocurrency and web3 industries are prime targets. watch nowAssistant Director in Charge Patrick Grandy, of the FBI's Los Angeles Field Office, called FaceStealer "a highly effective social engineering scheme capable of deceiving even the most experienced technical and security conscious computer user." "It exploits our trust in ubiquitous video conference platforms and valued personal relationships. If you can't imagine a scenario where you might fall prey to it, you are not thinking creatively enough," Grandy added."North Korea's government bankrolls its rogue regime and illicit weapons program through cryptocurrency theft," Principal Deputy Assistant Attorney General for National Security M. Scott Proctor said in a statement. "America will fight back against that corrupt regime's effort to profit through cybercrime. The National Security Division will use every tool at its disposal to seize and return North Korea's ill-gotten gains."

schema.headline: U.S. seizes $1.2 billion in cryptocurrency stolen from Binance

title: Is a bottom in for the Nasdaq-100? Charts to watch
description: (See the video above for Frank's complete chart breakdown.)Is the Nasdaq-100's recent bounce a sign that the bottom is in? We're going to look at seve
body: (See the video above for Frank's complete chart breakdown.)Is the Nasdaq-100's recent bounce a sign that the bottom is in? We're going to look at several charts to help answer that question.First, let's remember how we got here. In September, the NDX broke out from a bullish cup-and-handle pattern, producing a 33,200-upside target. That breakout quickly failed, however, and gave way to a bearish pattern that broke down aggressively two weeks ago.CappThesisThe decline brought the index relatively close to its 26,350 downside target before the current rebound began.CappThesisZooming out, it's telling to see where the bounce originated. Three important forms of support converged in the 25,000-26,000 area:The uptrend line extending from the early 2025 low through the early 2026 low.The 38.2% Fibonacci retracement of the entire 2025-2026 rally.The former 2025 highs, which represented resistance before becoming a key breakout zone earlier this year.This confluence of support helped encourage buying after a roughly 15% decline.For perspective, we also see what larger drawdowns of 20%, 30%, 40%, and 50% would look like … a lot worse.CappThesisThe following chart tracks NDX drawdowns from 52-week highs going back to just after the financial crisis. Only a handful of declines exceeded 20%, and three produced relatively quick reversals: late 2018, the Covid lows in 2020 and April 2025.Historically, buying into declines of approximately 15%–25% has generally paid off, even when additional downside occurred first (yellow highlights).The chart also highlights previous declines of 10%–16% in green, putting the current pullback into perspective.The major exception was 2022, when the NDX eventually declined nearly 36% over approximately 10 months ... a much worse outcome, which many investors are concerned could happen again now.CappThesisThat raises the key question: Are we experiencing another routine correction, or the early stages of a larger bear market?One important clue will be how far this bounce progresses.Any rally that fails to reclaim the previous highs could establish a significant lower high. Additional lower highs would provide stronger evidence of a developing, longer downtrend.We saw this in March 2022, when that first sharp rebound effort failed to reach the previous high before a much more severe decline followed.CappThesisThe bottom line: The current bounce is encouraging, particularly given where it originated and knowing how well buying prior 10-20% drawdowns has paid off.  From here, it's all about the follow through.  We don't need to see new highs right away, but any rally from here that's met with another wave of strong selling could reignite downside momentum.Frank Cappelleri is the founder and president of CappThesis, an independent research firm that helps active investors through time-tested chart and statistical analysis. Prior to starting CappThesis, he spent 25 years on Wall Street as an equity sales trader, technical analyst, research sales specialist and desk strategist.DISCLOSURES: (None)All opinions expressed by the CNBC Pro contributors are solely their opinions and do not reflect the opinions of CNBC, or its parent company or affiliates, and may have been previously disseminated by them on television, radio, internet or another medium.THIS CONTENT IS PROVIDED FOR INFORMATIONAL PURPOSES ONLY AND DOES NOT CONSTITUTE FINANCIAL, INVESTMENT, TAX OR LEGAL ADVICE OR A RECOMMENDATION TO BUY ANY SECURITY OR OTHER FINANCIAL ASSET. title: Supreme Court agrees to hear Robinhood challenge to IPO information omission lawsuit
description: A Robinhood logo is displayed at the Robinhood Markets, Inc. event in New York City, U.S., March 4, 2026.   David Dee Delgado | ReutersThe Supreme Cou
body: A Robinhood logo is displayed at the Robinhood Markets, Inc. event in New York City, U.S., March 4, 2026.   David Dee Delgado | ReutersThe Supreme Court on Friday agreed to hear a case in which Robinhood seeks to block a class-action lawsuit over the omission of interim financial data from the online broker's initial public offering in 2021.Robinhood wants the Supreme Court to overturn a ruling by the 9th Circuit U.S. Court of Appeals that revived a lawsuit by investors against the company and firms involved with the IPO, including Goldman Sachs and J.P. Morgan Securities.A San Francisco federal court judge had previously dismissed the lawsuit.The Trump administration and the Securities and Exchange Commission had urged the Supreme Court to hear Robinhood's appeal."We are pleased the Supreme Court has agreed to hear our case and look forward to presenting our argument," a Robinhood spokesperson said in a statement.CNBC has requested comment from the attorneys representing the plaintiffs in the case.Robinhood's IPO came on the heels of a surge in investor interest during the Covid-19 pandemic in so-called meme stocks, and trading in the crypto asset dogecoin.In July 2021, Robinhood conducted its IPO, "for which it prepared a registration statement" that "contained only limited information about Robinhood's performance during the second quarter of 2021," the 9th Circuit panel that heard the case noted."After the initial public offering, Robinhood reported financial results from that second quarter, and its stock price dropped," the panel wrote.The investors who sued Robinhood and the other defendants alleged the registration statement omitted material information it was legally required to disclose.

schema.headline: Supreme Court agrees to hear Robinhood challenge to IPO information omission lawsuit

title: CFTC Chair Selig tells CNBC crypto industry is embracing agency rules as legislation hopes fade
description: watch nowThe Commodity Futures Trading Commission is already seeing demand from crypto exchanges planning to opt in to its newly proposed rules govern
body: watch nowThe Commodity Futures Trading Commission is already seeing demand from crypto exchanges planning to opt in to its newly proposed rules governing digital assets, according to Chairman Michael Selig.The commodities regulator in October proposed rules aimed at preventing abuse in crypto markets and codifying crypto transaction rules under a federal rulebook. In the announcement, Selig said the move was a "critical step" in ensuring the United States remains the crypto capital of the world.Speaking this week at Cantor Convergence, an annual FinTech conference held in Miami Beach, Selig told CNBC in an exclusive interview that many of the major crypto exchanges are already registered with the CFTC because they offer financial derivatives, including perpetual futures, on their platforms and would now be able to add spot trading. "We're also getting interest from new entrants who say, 'Look, signing up with 50 different state regimes is tough. We'd rather come to one regulator and get a license at the CFTC' so those new entrants are lining up to come register with us as well," he added. After the Clarity Act, a comprehensive market structure bill that established a regulatory framework for digital assets, stalled in the Senate in September, the CFTC and the SEC moved to establish federal frameworks using their existing statutory authorities."We need to protect our markets and protect our customers using those markets so we'll continue to do exactly that in the wake of the Clarity Act failing to get the votes it needed to get to the president's desk during the current Congress," Selig said."Our statute does provide for authority of the agencies to register exchanges that want to offer margined, leveraged, or financed crypto assets or other types of commodity trading so we're utilizing that authority to allow our existing exchanges to begin offering these products under a regulated framework," he said.Selig added that the oversight is opt-in for exchanges that are not currently offering margin leveraged financing, which is not permitted under existing state regimes.watch nowBut the CFTC's new rules could face new scrutiny and oversight in 2027, with Democrats set to take control of the House and Senate after the midterms. Selig told CNBC he hopes the U.S. won't see a wave of software developers moving offshore, as many crypto businesses threatened to do under the Biden administration."I really hope that we learned lessons from the last several years in this space," he said.Crypto firms were at odds with Washington during the Biden administration, asking for clear operating rules, while also facing lawsuits brought by the SEC under former chair Gary Gensler's leadership. That shifted after President Donald Trump's 2024 victory."I do hope that we can work together with both sides of the aisle to protect software developers who want to do the right thing," Selig said, adding that those looking to commit crimes and engage in fraud should be held accountable.When asked whether he's prepared for increased scrutiny from Congress in 2027, Selig said, "Congress will do its job investigating where it needs to investigate.""I'm happy to answer any questions that Congress has for me just as I would answer Congress' questions today as I've done before hearing committees several times already," he said.Selig has also faced heat from Democrats for his handling of prediction markets. In February, 23 Democratic senators sent a letter to Chairman Selig urging him to reverse the agency's greenlighting of prediction markets.Selig has argued that prediction platforms are federally regulated as more states try to rein them in. The CFTC has sued several states to defend what the agency views as its exclusive jurisdiction to regulate event contracts, which it classifies as swaps."We're going to fight this up to the Supreme Court if that's where it's going," Selig said. "Our view on the statute is that we have exclusive jurisdiction over these markets, and I will not allow for states to go bring lawsuits against our exchanges, claiming that they're unlicensed gambling."— CNBC's Tanaya Macheel contributed to this report.

schema.headline: CFTC Chair Selig tells CNBC crypto industry is embracing agency rules as legislation hopes fade
